name: Junction Box
tagline: Where cables meet. Every joint has to live in an enclosure you can still open in ten years’ time.
terminals: Terminal block — one way per conductor
Earth — a linked earth terminal for every cable
Cable entries — knockouts or glands around the rim
parts: Enclosure — round or rectangular, with a screw-down lid
Terminal block — a strip connector, one screw per conductor
Cable entries — knockouts or glands that grip the sheath
Lid fixing screw — keeps the lid on and the joint enclosed
Base fixing holes — screws that anchor the box to the joist or wall
safety: A joint buried in plaster, under floorboards or inside a wall cavity is not a joint — it is a fault waiting to be found. Every connection must be in an accessible enclosure, or made with a maintenance-free connector rated to be buried. Screw terminals must stay accessible for inspection and testing.

points.label: Enclosure
points.detail: The box exists so the joint can be found and inspected later. It must be fixed (not floating in a void), big enough for the conductors without cramming, and rated for the environment — an IP rating outdoors, and a fire-rated box where it sits in a ceiling.

points.label: Terminal block
points.detail: One way of the strip per conductor, with every live, neutral and earth made separately. The screws must grip the conductor, not the insulation, and each connection gets a gentle pull test before the lid goes on.

points.label: Cable entries
points.detail: Knockouts or glands sized to the cable. The sheath should be gripped and should enter far enough that the insulation is still inside the box — bare conductor poking out of a gland is how a joint ends up shorting to the box.

points.label: Lid fixing screw
points.detail: The lid is part of the protection: it stops fingers and screws reaching live terminals. If the lid will not sit flat, the conductors are not dressed in properly — do not force it.
